content_voiceover: This page covers carrier counseling and a classic pediatric bleeding disorder pitfall. The first case is a pregnant carrier of severe hemophilia A whose factor eight level is actually high, one thirty five percent, because pregnancy itself raises factor eight. She's carrying a single male fetus. The key teaching points are that her son's risk of being affected depends on the father's genotype only if we're talking about an X-linked recessive pattern from her side, but more importantly, amniocentesis is not absolutely contraindicated by bleeding risk here since her own factor level is normal, and neuraxial anesthesia like an epidural is not automatically off limits either, it depends on her actual coagulation status at delivery, not simply on carrier status. What actually should be avoided in a potentially affected male fetus is instrumented delivery, forceps or vacuum extraction, because of the risk of intracranial or scalp hemorrhage in a baby who may have severe hemophilia. The second vignette is a classic exam pattern, an eight month old girl with a large scalp hematoma after a minor bump, hemoglobin dropping to seven, but normal platelet count and normal PT and aPTT. The mother also recalls prior oozing from the umbilical stump. Normal PT and aPTT rules out the common factor deficiencies like hemophilia A, B, or C, all of which would prolong aPTT. Delayed umbilical cord bleeding with normal screening coagulation tests is the textbook clue for factor thirteen deficiency, because factor thirteen acts downstream of the standard clotting cascade and isn't picked up by PT or aPTT at all.
keypoints: Pregnancy raises maternal factor VIII, so a carrier's own level can look falsely reassuring
Amniocentesis and epidural are not automatically contraindicated by carrier status alone
Avoid forceps or vacuum extraction if the male fetus may be affected
Normal PT/aPTT with bleeding excludes hemophilia A, B, and C
Umbilical stump bleeding plus normal PT/aPTT points to factor XIII deficiency
keypoint_voiceover: Remember these two patterns. First, being a hemophilia carrier does not automatically forbid amniocentesis or epidural anesthesia, those depend on the mother's actual coagulation status, but instrumented delivery should be avoided if the male fetus could be affected. Second, when you see normal PT and aPTT despite significant bleeding, especially with a history of delayed umbilical stump bleeding, think factor thirteen deficiency, since it sits downstream of the pathways those two screening tests measure.
